title: Step 1: Create a safe branch and baseline — inline video playback
body:
Implement Step 1 of the Boru Inline Video Playback Implementation Guide (PDF: /home/dan/.hermes/kanban/boards/iroh-gossip-chat/attachments/t_099fd2a7/Boru_Inline_Video_Player_Implementation_Guide.pdf).

GOAL: Establish a clean starting point and prove that any later failure was introduced by the video feature, not inherited from the existing codebase.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Create a dedicated feature branch for inline video playback (e.g. feature/inline-video-player).
2. Build Boru in the same configuration normally used for development and record the exact command.
3. Run the existing automated tests and record any pre-existing failures without fixing unrelated problems.
4. Manually verify sending and receiving normal text, images, and generic files in both rooms and direct messages.
5. Capture screenshots or notes of current attachment rendering so later UI changes can be compared.
6. Add a short implementation note under the project documentation describing the branch, build command, and baseline status.

GUARDRAILS:
- Do not refactor production code in this step.
- Do not update unrelated dependencies merely because newer versions exist.
- Treat current failing tests as baseline only when they can be reproduced before any feature code changes.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- The clean branch builds successfully, or the exact pre-existing blocker is documented.
- Existing message and attachment flows have been manually exercised.
- No functional source-code change has been introduced.
- The baseline build and test commands are written down.

CHECKPOINT COMMIT: chore(video): establish inline playback baseline

title: Step 2: Map Boru message and attachment architecture — inline video playback

GOAL: Find the real extension points before writing implementation code.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Trace a received attachment from network/message deserialization through persistence and into the chat message renderer.
2. Trace a sent attachment from the file picker through transfer, persistence, and rendering.
3. Identify the message identity type used to uniquely address one message across room and direct-message views.
4. Identify where attachment MIME type, extension, local path, content address, download progress, and verification state are stored.
5. Identify the Iced message/update/view components that render attachment messages and handle interaction events.
6. Identify the scrollable chat component and determine whether message widgets are recreated on every view pass.
7. Write a concise architecture note listing the files and types that should be extended in later steps.

GUARDRAILS:
- Do not add a second attachment model.
- Do not store decoder objects inside persistent message records.
- Do not assume file extensions are trustworthy when a MIME or content probe already exists.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- The architecture note names the exact types and files involved in sent and received attachments.
- The agent can identify where local-file readiness becomes true.
- The agent can identify a stable message or attachment key suitable for player coordination.
- No speculative large refactor has been committed.

GOAL: Allow Boru to distinguish playable video attachments without changing how attachments are transferred.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Add a small media classification function or enum that can represent at least Video and NonVideo.
2. Classify using trusted or normalized MIME metadata when available, with a conservative extension fallback only where necessary.
3. Keep unknown media as a generic file rather than guessing that it is playable.
4. Use the same classification path for sent and received attachments.
5. Add unit tests for common supported and unsupported examples, including uppercase extensions and missing MIME data.
6. Route classified video attachments to a temporary video-card rendering branch that may still show a placeholder.

GUARDRAILS:
- Do not change network payload compatibility unless the existing protocol genuinely lacks required metadata.
- Do not treat a filename as proof that a file is safe or decodable.
- Do not remove the generic download/open behaviour; it remains the fallback.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- MP4, WebM, and other intentionally supported types are classified consistently.
- Unknown or contradictory metadata falls back safely to a generic attachment.

GOAL: Separate durable media information from short-lived player state.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Define the minimum reusable metadata structure: duration, width, height, optional poster reference, media type, and probe status.

3. Define a stable VideoInstanceKey using conversation identity plus message or attachment identity.
4. Define ephemeral player UI state for idle, preparing, playing, paused, ended, and failed states.

- Keep optional metadata optional so old messages and partially downloaded files remain valid.
- Use stable identifiers rather than list positions or scroll indices.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- Old message data loads without panic or data loss.
- Persistent and ephemeral responsibilities are clearly separated.
- Every video message can be uniquely addressed.

- Keep cache deletion safe; cached posters must be reproducible.

GOAL: Keep chat scrolling smooth and release expensive resources when players are no longer useful.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Measure or detect whether the active video card is within or near the visible chat viewport using the best mechanism supported by the current Iced architecture.
2. Choose and document a policy for off-screen playback: pause immediately, pause after a threshold, or continue audio only when explicitly supported.
3. Destroy or suspend inactive player resources after a safe timeout or when they are far outside the viewport.
4. Keep lightweight state so returning to the message can show the correct poster or resume position according to policy.
5. Stop and clean up all video resources when the conversation view is destroyed or the application exits.
6. Test chats containing many video messages without activating them.
7. Test rapid scrolling while one video is playing.

GUARDRAILS:
- Do not construct a decoder simply because a card became visible.
- Do not keep an unlimited registry of inactive players.
- Do not let lifecycle cleanup delete or corrupt the underlying attachment file.
- Prefer a clear, predictable pause policy over hidden background playback.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- A chat containing many video cards remains responsive before any video is played.
- Scrolling an active video off-screen follows the documented policy.
- Returning to the card produces a coherent state rather than a blank or broken surface.
- Leaving the conversation or exiting Boru releases media resources.

title: Step 15: Harden security and file verification — inline video playback

GOAL: Ensure the new decoder path respects Boru's peer-to-peer trust boundaries.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Confirm that playback paths are derived only from Boru-managed, completed, verified local attachments.
2. Revalidate file existence and expected content identity immediately before creating the player.
3. Prevent path traversal or arbitrary URL playback through peer-controlled metadata.
4. Use local file APIs rather than passing filenames through a shell.
5. Apply reasonable limits to metadata probing and poster generation, including dimensions, duration parsing, and resource usage.
6. Document the decoder as an additional attack surface and ensure runtime libraries are kept within the project's dependency-update process.
7. Add negative tests for suspicious filenames, missing files, partial files, and content-identity mismatch.

GUARDRAILS:
- Never stream a peer-supplied URL directly into GStreamer.
- Never execute a player command through a shell.
- Never trust extension or MIME metadata as integrity verification.
- Do not weaken Boru's existing permission model for content-addressed files.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- Only verified local attachments can enter the inline decoder path.
- Path traversal and arbitrary URL attempts are rejected.
- A mismatched or replaced local file cannot be silently played as the verified attachment.
- Security assumptions and residual risks are documented.

title: Step 18: Profile, polish, and roll out safely — inline video playback
body:
Implement Step 18 of the Boru Inline Video Playback Implementation Guide (PDF: /home/dan/.hermes/kanban/boards/iroh-gossip-chat/attachments/t_099fd2a7/Boru_Inline_Video_Player_Implementation_Guide.pdf).

GOAL: Resolve performance and usability issues before enabling inline playback by default.

AGENT TASKS:
1. Profile initial chat load with many video cards, first playback startup, steady playback, seek operations, rapid scrolling, and repeated player switching.
2. Measure CPU, GPU where observable, memory, open file handles, and background threads before and after cleanup.
3. Fix resource leaks and excessive redraws without broad unrelated refactors.
4. Review spacing, controls, loading states, error states, dark/light theme behaviour, and narrow-window behaviour.
5. Keep the feature behind a switch until clean-environment packaging and the manual matrix pass.
6. Enable by default only after documenting supported formats, known limitations, and fallback behaviour.
7. Prepare a focused pull request containing architecture notes, screenshots, test evidence, packaging notes, and rollback instructions.

GUARDRAILS:
- Do not optimize by removing integrity checks or lifecycle cleanup.
- Do not merge unrelated UI redesigns into the playback change.
- Do not enable by default when the clean-machine runtime test is still failing.
- Do not leave temporary developer harnesses reachable in production builds.

ACCEPTANCE CHECKS:
- Inactive video cards add minimal overhead compared with ordinary attachment cards.
- One active player cleans up its resources after stop, navigation, and exit.
- The feature works in clean packaged builds and degrades gracefully when unavailable.
- The pull request is reviewable, reversible, and limited to inline playback and required support code.

CHECKPOINT COMMIT: feat(video): finalize inline playback rollout

title: Final release checklist: verify inline video playback end-to-end
body:
Run the final release checklist from the Boru Inline Video Playback Implementation Guide (PDF: /home/dan/.hermes/kanban/boards/iroh-gossip-chat/attachments/t_099fd2a7/Boru_Inline_Video_Player_Implementation_Guide.pdf). This is the acceptance gate after Steps 1-18 are complete.

Verify ALL of the following:
1. Inline playback works in both rooms and direct messages.
2. Videos can be watched completely without leaving the conversation.
3. Only verified local files enter the decoder path.
4. No autoplay occurs.
5. Only one video actively plays at a time.
6. Inactive cards do not create decoders.
7. Scroll-away and navigation lifecycle behaviour is predictable and tested.
8. Unsupported or corrupt media never crashes the chat view.
9. GStreamer/runtime dependencies work on a clean installation.
10. Text, image, and generic-file attachments retain their prior behaviour.
11. Supported formats and known limitations are documented.

STOP CONDITION (from the guide): The feature is not complete merely when a development MP4 plays. It is complete when inline playback, lifecycle cleanup, error recovery, security checks, packaging, and regression tests all pass in a normal packaged Boru build.

Report which checklist items pass/fail with evidence, and list any remaining gaps as follow-up tasks.
